title: Social Feed
summary: Post a message; see a timeline of posts from everyone you follow. Write-amplified rather than read-dominated, which inverts almost every decision the URL shortener made.

versions.label: 10K users
versions.trigger: Launch. Build the timeline by querying at read time — the obvious implementation, and correct at this size.
versions.note: This is fan-out on READ: assemble the timeline when someone asks for it. One join, no duplication, and a post is visible the instant it is written.

versions.label: 500K users
versions.trigger: Timeline assembly became the slowest endpoint. The same users refresh constantly and get an identical answer each time.
versions.note: The cache hides the cost but does not remove it. p99 barely moves, because the tail IS the miss path — and every new post invalidates the timeline of everyone who follows the author.

versions.label: 5M users
versions.trigger: A user following 2,000 accounts needed a 2,000-way merge on every refresh. Read-time assembly does not scale with follow count.
versions.note: The inversion: fan-out on WRITE. When you post, push the post id into every follower's precomputed feed. Reads become a single sequential read. The cost has moved from read time to write time — and it has been multiplied by your follower count.

versions.label: 20M users
versions.trigger: Fan-out on write made posting slow: the author waited while the system wrote to thousands of feeds.
versions.note: The author's request returns as soon as the post is durable. Fan-out happens behind a queue, so a post is visible to followers seconds later rather than instantly — which nobody notices, and which is the whole reason this is acceptable.

versions.label: Celebrity posts
versions.trigger: An account with 40M followers posted. That is 40M feed writes from a single request, and the fan-out queue backed up for hours behind it.
versions.note: The celebrity problem, and it is not an edge case — it is the defining constraint of every social product. Fan-out on write assumes follower counts are roughly uniform. They follow a power law, so the top 0.001% of accounts generate most of the total write volume.

versions.label: Hybrid fan-out
versions.trigger: Neither strategy works alone: write fan-out dies on celebrities, read fan-out dies on high follow counts.
versions.note: Push for the long tail, pull for the few. A timeline read is now a merge of one precomputed feed and a handful of celebrity queries. Slightly slower reads for everyone, in exchange for the write path never seeing a 40M-row insert.

versions.label: Media at scale
versions.trigger: Images and video dominated bandwidth and cost far more to serve than the text ever did.
versions.note: The timeline response carries URLs, not bytes. Media never touches the application tier — an app server that streams video is an app server doing the CDN's job at a hundred times the cost.

versions.label: Fan-out workers lost
versions.trigger: Design review: the fan-out workers stop. What does a user actually see?
versions.note: Nothing fails. Timelines still load, they just stop gaining new posts, and the backlog drains when workers return. That is graceful degradation earned by design — the same outage on the synchronous V3 architecture would have taken posting down entirely.

flows.label: Load timeline (fan-out on read)
flows.outcome: Two queries and an N-way merge, at read time, on every single refresh.

flows.label: Load timeline — cache hit
flows.outcome: Fast, until someone you follow posts and invalidates it.

flows.label: Load timeline — cache miss
flows.outcome: The full assembly cost reappears. This path is your p99, and caching did not remove it.

flows.label: Load timeline (precomputed)
flows.outcome: One sequential read of a ready-made list, then hydrate the post bodies. Independent of how many accounts you follow.

flows.label: Publish a post
flows.outcome: Returns as soon as the post is durable. The follower fan-out has not happened yet — and the author cannot tell.

flows.label: Fan-out (async, off the request path)
flows.outcome: One row inserted per follower. For a normal account that is hundreds; for a celebrity it is tens of millions.

flows.label: Load timeline (hybrid merge)
flows.outcome: Precomputed feed for the long tail, merged with live queries for the few celebrities you follow.

flows.label: Load an image
flows.outcome: Served at the edge. Never reaches your infrastructure — which is why media does not appear in your capacity plan.

flows.label: Load timeline while fan-out is down
flows.outcome: Serves normally from the last-written feed. The timeline is stale, not broken.

failures.effect: Every timeline is reassembled from scratch. At V2 that is catastrophic because assembly is the expensive path; from V3 on it barely matters, because reads are already precomputed.
Timelines cannot be read at all. Precomputing moved the read path onto this store, so losing it is losing the product's main screen.
Timelines stop gaining new posts but keep serving what they already hold. Posting still works. The backlog drains when workers return — graceful degradation earned by putting fan-out behind a queue.
Posts are accepted and durably stored but never reach anyone's timeline — and unlike a worker outage, the work is not waiting anywhere to be replayed.
Follow and unfollow stop. Reading still works from V3 on, because the follower list was consulted at write time rather than read time.
Feed rows still exist but there is nothing to hydrate them with — the timeline renders as a list of ids with no content. Posting fails.
Text timelines are unaffected; media falls back to origin and the bandwidth bill becomes the incident.
